title: My Son Donated His Heart Before He Died. At His Funeral, A Stranger Revealed A Secret About My Late Husband That Changed Everything.

blocks.text: My name is Meredith Price, and I used to believe the worst thing that could happen to a mother was burying her child.
Sometimes, the worst thing happens afterward, when someone hands you a piece of paper that makes you question everything you thought you knew about the people you loved.
Four years before I lost my son, I lost my husband.

Patrick Price was the kind of man who could make an ordinary Tuesday feel like a celebration. He loved terrible jokes, Sunday pancakes, and taking Colin fishing even though neither of them ever caught anything worth keeping.
When Patrick died unexpectedly from a heart attack, our little family was shattered.
He didn’t cry at the funeral. He simply stood beside me, holding my hand so tightly that my fingers went numb.
That night, he came into my bedroom, climbed onto the edge of the bed, and said something I’ll never forget.
“Don’t worry, Mom. I’ll take care of you now.”
But he became my reason to get out of bed every morning.

Colin grew into a remarkable young man. He was clever, sarcastic, compassionate, and endlessly curious about how things worked. He could spend hours taking apart broken electronics and putting them back together.
He wanted to design medical equipment that could save lives.
I used to tease him that he would probably build me a robot to do the dishes.
“Only if you promise not to complain about its cooking, Mom.”
I never imagined those conversations would become memories I would spend the rest of my life protecting.
The diagnosis that destroyed our future
Shortly after his eighteenth birthday, Colin collapsed in the kitchen.
I was preparing dinner when I heard a terrible crash.
I turned around and found him on the floor.
His eyes were open, but he couldn’t respond.
At the hospital, doctors ran test after test. Specialists examined him, ordered scans, and spoke in hushed voices outside his room.
Finally, one neurologist asked me to sit down.
He explained that Colin had a rare, rapidly progressing neurological disease.
The condition was attacking his nervous system, and the progression was unpredictable.
I researched hospitals, contacted specialists, and spent nights searching for experimental treatments.
I sold my jewelry. I emptied my savings.
Every time someone told me there was little hope, I found another question to ask.
Colin, however, seemed to understand his situation much sooner than I did.
One evening, while I was helping him eat dinner, he looked at me and smiled.
“Mom, you know you don’t have to fight every battle for me, right?”
“Don’t say that. We’re going to find something.”
“I know. But if we can’t, I want you to promise me something.”
“I want to donate whatever I can. If my organs can help someone else live, I want that.”
“Mom, I don’t want my last chapter to be about what I lost. I want it to be about what I can still give.”
I held him and promised I would respect his wishes.
I had no idea how much that promise would eventually change my life.
His final gift
There were days when he could barely speak. Other days, he seemed almost like his old self, joking with nurses and asking whether the hospital cafeteria had finally learned how to make decent coffee.
He turned nineteen in his hospital room.
I brought a small chocolate cake with one candle.
We sang together, although I couldn’t finish the song without crying.
He blew out the candle and whispered his birthday wish.
Three weeks later, his condition took a devastating turn.
The doctors explained that his neurological disease had caused irreversible damage. His body was failing, and there was nothing more they could do to stop it.
After the medical team carefully assessed his eligibility, his heart was recovered for transplantation and offered to a patient who urgently needed it.
I only knew that somewhere, someone might get another chance because my son had chosen to give what he could.
It was the only thing keeping me standing.
The stranger at the funeral
Colin’s funeral took place on a rainy Thursday.
His teachers came. His classmates came. Friends from the hospital came. Even the local engineering club sent flowers.
I stood near his photograph, thanking people mechanically.
I couldn’t remember most of their faces.
Then I noticed a woman standing near the entrance.
She looked to be in her forties. She wore a dark blue coat and held a small envelope against her chest.
Eventually, after most guests had left, she walked toward me.
“My name is Elaine Carter. I think my daughter may have received your son’s heart.”
“Her name is Sophie. She’s eighteen. She was born with a serious heart condition. For years, we were told she might not survive without a transplant.”
“She’s alive. She’s recovering. And every time I hear her heartbeat, I think about the boy who gave her that chance.”
Elaine reached into her handbag and removed an envelope.
